title: Chromatic Harmony
intro: Beyond secondary dominants, tonal music borrows chords from the parallel minor, colours the predominant with the Neapolitan sixth and the augmented sixth chords, and decorates with common-tone diminished sevenths. These are the sounds of the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

blocks.text: A major key can borrow chords from its parallel minor: iv (Fm in C), ii°, ♭VI (A♭), ♭VII (B♭), ♭III (E♭) and the minor tonic itself. The borrowed ♭6̂ (A♭) is the key ingredient: it darkens the predominant (iv, iiø7) and falls expressively to 5̂. In rock, ♭VII and ♭VI are everyday chords: I–♭VII–IV (the 'Mixolydian' rock cadence), ♭VI–♭VII–I (the 'Mario cadence'). A minor piece ending on a major tonic chord uses the opposite borrowing: the Picardy third.

examples.label: Picardy third: iv–V–I in C minor

blocks.text: The Neapolitan is a major triad on the lowered second degree, ♭II: in C, D♭ F A♭. It almost always appears in first inversion (N6, with F in the bass) as a predominant leading to V, often through a cadential 6/4. Its characteristic motion is ♭2̂ falling a diminished third to the leading tone (D♭ to B). It is most at home in minor keys; Beethoven's 'Moonlight' Sonata uses it in the first movement.

Augmented sixth chords are predominants built around the interval of an augmented sixth between ♭6̂ in the bass and ♯4̂ above, which expand outward by a semitone each to the octave on 5̂: in C, A♭ and F♯ open to G and G. Three 'national' types add different notes:

items: French (Fr+6): ♭6̂, 1̂, 2̂, ♯4̂: A♭ C D F♯. Its whole-tone sound is distinctive.

German (Ger+6): ♭6̂, 1̂, ♭3̂, ♯4̂: A♭ C E♭ F♯. Sounds exactly like A♭7, so it can be respelled as a dominant seventh for enharmonic modulation. Resolving it straight to V gives parallel fifths (A♭–E♭ to G–D), so it usually goes through the cadential 6/4 first.

widget.title: Augmented sixths resolving to V in C

blocks.text: A fully diminished seventh can decorate a major chord by sharing one note with it: C–(D♯ F♯ A C)–C in C major, where three voices move by step out of the C chord and back while C holds. It has no dominant function at all; it is a chromatic neighbour chord. It is a favourite of Romantic and barbershop music.

Play the bass line ♭6̂–5̂ (A♭–G) in octaves with the left hand and the three augmented sixth chords above it in the right hand. The bass and the top voice (F♯–G) move in contrary motion by semitone, the sound that makes these chords so final-sounding.

blocks.title: Spell
blocks.text: In D minor, spell the Neapolitan sixth and the German augmented sixth.
solution: ♭II in D is E♭ major: E♭ G B♭; N6 puts G in the bass: G B♭ E♭.
Ger+6: ♭6̂ = B♭ (in D minor 6̂ is already B♭), 1̂ = D, ♭3̂ = F, ♯4̂ = G♯: B♭ D F G♯, resolving outward to A–A.
blocks.answer: N6 = G B♭ E♭; Ger+6 = B♭ D F G♯

blocks.title: Enharmonic
blocks.text: The German sixth in C (A♭ C E♭ F♯) sounds like what dominant seventh, and to what key would that dominant resolve?
solution: Respelling F♯ as G♭ gives A♭ C E♭ G♭, the dominant seventh of D♭. So the same sound can lead to C (as Ger+6, via G) or to D♭ major (as V7).
